q: Sodium reacts with cold water to give:
x: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. The metal displaces hydrogen from water and leaves an alkaline solution.

q: Lithium burns in oxygen to form only the normal oxide, Li₂O, mainly because:
o: Lithium has the lowest ionisation energy in Group I
The very small Li⁺ ion has high polarising power and cannot stabilise the large peroxide ion
Lithium does not react with oxygen at all
The Li⁺ ion is larger than the other Group I ions
x: Small cations with high charge density distort and destabilise large anions such as O₂²⁻ and O₂⁻. Larger ions like K⁺ can stabilise them, so K forms a superoxide.

q: Which shows the correct order of increasing vigour of reaction with water?
x: Down Group I the atoms get larger and ionisation energy falls, so the outer electron is lost more easily and reaction with water becomes more violent.

q: Which alkali metal reacts directly with nitrogen to form a nitride?
x: Lithium forms Li₃N, an anomalous property it shares with magnesium (diagonal relationship). The other alkali metals do not form nitrides directly.

q: When sodium burns in excess oxygen, the main product is:
x: Sodium mainly forms sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂, containing the O₂²⁻ ion. Lithium forms the normal oxide Li₂O, and potassium and heavier metals form superoxides.

q: Which Group I chloride shows the greatest covalent character?
x: Li⁺ is the smallest Group I ion and polarises the Cl⁻ electron cloud most, so LiCl has some covalent character, e.g. it dissolves in organic solvents.

q: Potassium burns in excess oxygen to form potassium superoxide, KO₂. What is the oxidation number of oxygen in KO₂?
x: K is +1, so the two O atoms together are −1, giving −½ each. This is the superoxide ion O₂⁻; −1 is the value in peroxides and −2 in normal oxides.

q: Which Group II chloride is covalent, has a low melting point and forms polymeric chains in the solid?
x: The tiny Be²⁺ ion has very high polarising power, so BeCl₂ is covalent. The chlorides lower in the group are ionic solids.

q: Group I metals (M) react with chlorine to form chlorides with the general formula:
x: Group I metals form M⁺ ions, and chlorine forms Cl⁻, so the chloride is MCl, e.g. 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.

q: Which Group II oxide is amphoteric?
x: BeO reacts with both acids and bases. The other Group II oxides are basic, and their basic strength increases down the group.

q: Sodium peroxide is added to ice-cold water. The products are:
x: Na₂O₂ + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂O₂ in cold water. The peroxide ion takes H⁺ to give H₂O₂; hydrogen gas is given by the metal, not the peroxide.

q: Which property is shared by lithium and magnesium (diagonal relationship)?
o: Both form peroxides when burnt in excess oxygen
Both react explosively with cold water
Both burn in air to form a nitride as well as a normal oxide
Both show a valency of two in their compounds
x: Li and Mg both form Li₃N and Mg₃N₂ besides the normal oxides Li₂O and MgO. Neither forms peroxides readily, both react only slowly with cold water, and Li has valency one.

q: What volume of hydrogen at STP is produced when 2.3 g of sodium reacts completely with water? (Na = 23; 1 mol gas = 22.4 dm³)
x: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Moles of Na = 2.3/23 = 0.1, giving 0.05 mol H₂ = 0.05 × 22.4 = 1.12 dm³. Ignoring the 2 : 1 ratio gives 2.24 dm³.

q: Potassium reacts with water more vigorously than sodium because potassium:
o: Has a higher nuclear charge, which holds its outer electron more tightly
Has two outer electrons while sodium has one
Forms a protective oxide layer that sodium lacks
Has a larger atom and a lower ionisation energy, so it loses its outer electron more easily
x: The outer 4s electron of K is farther from the nucleus and better shielded than the 3s electron of Na, so it is removed more easily and K reacts faster.

q: When magnesium is heated in steam, the products are:
x: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂. Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water but readily with steam.

q: Which Group II carbonate decomposes at the lowest temperature on heating?
x: Thermal stability of Group II carbonates increases down the group. The small Mg²⁺ ion has the highest polarising power and distorts the carbonate ion most, so MgCO₃ decomposes most easily. BaCO₃ is the most stable, the reversed-trend slip.

q: Magnesium nitrate is heated strongly. The products are:
x: Group II nitrates decompose to the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen: 2Mg(NO₃)₂ → 2MgO + 4NO₂ + O₂ (brown fumes seen). Forming a nitrite and oxygen is what sodium nitrate does, the usual mix-up.

q: Sodium nitrate is heated strongly. The products are:
x: Nitrates of sodium and the heavier alkali metals give the nitrite and oxygen only: 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂, with no brown gas. The oxide, NO₂ and O₂ are given by Group II nitrates and by LiNO₃.

q: Which of these Group II sulphates is the most soluble in water?
x: Solubility of Group II sulphates decreases down the group: MgSO₄ is freely soluble, CaSO₄ sparingly soluble and BaSO₄ practically insoluble (hence its use as the test precipitate for sulphate). Picking BaSO₄ reverses the trend, confusing it with the hydroxides.

q: Which of these Group II hydroxides is the most soluble in water?
x: Solubility of Group II hydroxides increases down the group, so Ba(OH)₂ is the most soluble and Mg(OH)₂ is only sparingly soluble (milk of magnesia is a suspension). This trend is the opposite of the sulphates, which is the usual source of error.

q: A 20 g mixture of CaCO₃ and NaCl is heated strongly to constant mass and loses 4.4 g. What is the percentage by mass of CaCO₃ in the mixture? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
x: Only CaCO₃ decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. 4.4 g CO₂ = 0.1 mol, so 0.1 mol CaCO₃ = 10 g, which is 10/20 = 50 %. Taking the mass loss itself as the CaCO₃ gives 22 %.

q: Which compound gives off carbon dioxide when heated gently in a test tube over a Bunsen burner?
x: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ on gentle heating. Group I carbonates such as Na₂CO₃ and K₂CO₃ are stable to Bunsen temperatures, and NaCl does not decompose.

q: In the Downs cell for making sodium, calcium chloride is mixed with the sodium chloride mainly to:
o: Lower the melting point of the electrolyte
Act as a catalyst at the cathode
Prevent sodium from reacting with water
x: Pure NaCl melts at about 801 °C; adding CaCl₂ lowers the melting point to about 600 °C, saving energy and reducing sodium vaporisation. There is no water in the cell, and CaCl₂ is not a catalyst.

q: In the Downs cell, the anode at which chlorine is liberated is made of:
x: The central anode is graphite, which resists attack by chlorine; the surrounding cathode, where sodium is discharged, is iron. Choosing iron mixes up the anode and cathode.

q: In the Nelson cell, brine is electrolysed in a perforated steel cathode lined with asbestos. The main purpose of the asbestos diaphragm is to:
o: Absorb the hydrogen formed at the cathode
Keep the chlorine formed at the anode away from the NaOH and H₂ formed at the cathode
Convert sodium metal into sodium hydroxide
x: Cl₂ would react with NaOH (giving NaCl and NaOCl) and with H₂, so the diaphragm keeps the anode and cathode products apart while letting the brine percolate through. No sodium metal forms in aqueous electrolysis.

q: In the Nelson cell, 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂. What mass of sodium hydroxide is produced along with 71 g of chlorine? (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
x: 71 g Cl₂ = 1 mol, and the equation gives 2 mol NaOH per mol Cl₂: 2 × 40 = 80 g. Using a 1:1 ratio gives 40 g; 117 g is the mass of NaCl used, not NaOH formed.

q: Gypsum is heated to about 120 °C to make plaster of Paris. The formula of plaster of Paris is:
x: Gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O, loses three-quarters of its water at about 120 °C to give (CaSO₄)₂·H₂O, i.e. CaSO₄·½H₂O. CaSO₄·2H₂O is gypsum itself, and anhydrous CaSO₄ (dead-burnt plaster) forms only on stronger heating.

q: In a lime kiln limestone is heated: CaCO₃ ⇌ CaO + CO₂. Why is a current of air blown through to remove CO₂ continuously?
o: CO₂ acts as a catalyst poison for the decomposition
Removing CO₂ shifts the equilibrium to the right, giving more quicklime
Removing CO₂ lowers the temperature needed for slaking
CO₂ would react with the air to form carbon monoxide
x: By Le Chatelier's principle, removing a product drives the reversible decomposition forward, so more CaO is obtained. If CO₂ stayed, CaO and CO₂ would recombine to CaCO₃. There is no catalyst involved.

q: What mass of water is lost when 344 g of gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O, is completely converted into plaster of Paris, (CaSO₄)₂·H₂O? (Ca = 40, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)
x: Gypsum = 172 g mol⁻¹, so 344 g = 2 mol, holding 4 mol H₂O. Plaster of Paris keeps ½ H₂O per CaSO₄, i.e. 1 mol for 2 mol CaSO₄, so 3 mol water = 54 g is lost. Assuming all water is lost gives 72 g.

q: Unlike the nitrates of the other alkali metals, lithium nitrate on heating gives:
x: Because the small Li⁺ ion polarises the nitrate ion strongly, LiNO₃ decomposes like a Group II nitrate (diagonal relationship with Mg): 4LiNO₃ → 2Li₂O + 4NO₂ + O₂. The nitrite and oxygen are the products for NaNO₃ and KNO₃.
